Why the web keeps asking if you are human

Web infrastructure companies have spent the past year tightening the checks that stand between automated clients and the sites they protect, and readers increasingly meet an interstitial that says Just a moment... before a page appears.

The screens, which often read Performing security verification or Checking your browser, are shown while a service decides whether a visitor is a person. Publishers say the checks cut scraping costs, while researchers say they also block accessibility tools and archives.

At the same time, European regulators have pressed sites to make cookie banners honest: a Reject all button must be as easy to find as Accept all, and pre-ticked boxes are not consent. Several national authorities fined publishers this year for walls that hid the refusal option.

Paywalls are changing too. More newspapers now mark subscriber-only articles in their structured data, which lets search engines tell a paywall from cloaking, and some offer a metered number of free articles each month before asking readers to subscribe to continue reading.

Analysts expect the three trends to meet in the browser: a reader may see a consent dialog, a verification screen and a subscription prompt on the same visit, and each is designed to be answered by a person rather than a program.

The industry group behind the new guidance said it would publish test pages so that tool makers can check how their software reports each kind of wall, rather than guessing from an empty page.
